summary: The WebSocket Protocol is an Internet standard that lets a program, usually web page code running in a browser, hold a two-way connection with a server that has agreed to it. It specifies an opening handshake that starts as an ordinary web request, a message framing layer over the Transmission Control Protocol, address forms for plain and encrypted connections, and a check of the page origin. It leaves everything above the connection to others: what the messages mean is left to named application protocols called subprotocols, and how a client proves who it is is left to ordinary web mechanisms. It offers registered extensions and subprotocols and a version number agreed during the handshake. A trap for a standards audience is that it carries text and binary messages between two endpoints and nothing more, so it says nothing about worlds, shared state, media or identity; a system that uses it still has to define all of those itself.
